lead: Principal component analysis (PCA) changes coordinates. It replaces the original features with new, uncorrelated axes called principal components. The first axis points along the largest spread in the data, the second along the next largest spread at right angles to the first, and so on. Keeping only the first few axes gives a smaller feature set with most of the information. PCA is used to compress data, remove redundancy, plot high-dimensional data in two dimensions, and speed up models before classification or clustering.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for unlabeled data, and Unit 1 for vectors, matrices, eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

sections.h3: Centre the data, then measure spread

blocks.text: PCA starts with a data matrix X. It has n rows, one per sample, and d columns, one per feature. The symbol d is the original number of features. A row might hold a customer's age and monthly spend; a column is one feature across all customers.
Subtract the mean of each column. After this, every column has mean zero. Centring matters because PCA studies spread around the mean, not distance from zero.

blocks.where: X is the n×d mean-centred matrix; Xᵀ is its transpose; C is the d×d covariance matrix. The diagonal entry C_jj is the variance of feature j, and C_jk is the covariance between features j and k.

blocks.text: The covariance matrix is symmetric. It records how features move together. A positive off-diagonal entry means two features rise together; a negative entry means one rises while the other falls. PCA now looks for directions in which this matrix shows large spread.

items: Mean-centre each feature. Scale each feature to unit variance if the features use different units.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of C.
Sort the eigenvectors by their eigenvalues, largest first.
Keep the first k eigenvectors as columns of V_k and compute Z = X V_k.

blocks.text: An eigenvector v of C is a direction that C does not rotate. It only stretches v by a number λ, the eigenvalue. Write this as C v = λ v. For PCA, take v as a unit vector, so vᵀv = 1.

blocks.where: C is the d×d covariance matrix; v_i is the i-th unit eigenvector; λ_i is its eigenvalue.

blocks.text: Because C is symmetric, its eigenvectors are orthogonal. The first principal component v_1 has the largest λ_1. The variance of the data along v_1 equals λ_1. The second component v_2 is the direction of next largest variance among directions at right angles to v_1, and so on.

Total variance is the sum of all eigenvalues, Σ λ_i. The explained variance ratio of component i is λ_i / Σ λ_j. If the first three ratios are 0.50, 0.30 and 0.10, the first three components keep 90% of the variance. The remaining components carry 10%.
explained variance ratio_i = λ_i / Σ_j λ_j
blocks.where: λ_i is the eigenvalue of component i; the denominator sums all d eigenvalues.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this transform the Karhunen–Loève transform. The name changes; the calculation is the same.

The projection is Z = X V_k. X is the centred n×d matrix. V_k is the d×k matrix whose columns are the first k unit eigenvectors. Z is the n×k score matrix: each row is the same sample written in k new coordinates. The columns of Z are uncorrelated.

Scaling is a separate choice. If one feature is income in rupees and another is height in metres, income variance may be huge only because of its unit. Standardise each column to mean zero and standard deviation one before PCA. If all features share a unit and a meaningful scale, centring alone is often enough.

For large d, do not build C. Use the singular value decomposition X = U S Vᵀ. The columns of V are the principal directions, and the squared singular values divided by n−1 are the eigenvalues of C. Software libraries follow this route because it is numerically stable.
PCA is unsupervised: it never sees class labels. It keeps directions of high variance, which may or may not separate classes. For a supervised projection that uses labels, see Chapter 4.7.

figure.caption: The flow shows the order of operations; the eigenvalue step and the sort step decide which directions survive.

spec.title: PCA steps
spec.aria: PCA mean-centres the data, forms the covariance matrix, computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors, sorts components by variance and projects data onto the first k.

examples.question: A two-feature dataset is already mean-centred. Its covariance matrix is C = [[4, 3], [3, 4]]. Find both eigenvalues, the unit eigenvector for the first principal component, and the explained variance ratio of the first component.
steps: The characteristic equation is det(C − λI) = 0. For this 2×2 matrix: (4−λ)(4−λ) − 3×3 = 0, so λ² − 8λ + 7 = 0.
Solve λ² − 8λ + 7 = 0. The roots are λ = (8 ± √(64−28))/2 = (8 ± 6)/2. Thus λ₁ = 7 and λ₂ = 1.
For λ₁ = 7, solve (C − 7I)v = 0. The first row gives (4−7)x + 3y = 0, so −3x + 3y = 0, hence x = y. A unit vector is v₁ = (1, 1)/√2.
For λ₂ = 1, the first row gives (4−1)x + 3y = 0, so 3x + 3y = 0, hence y = −x. A unit vector is v₂ = (1, −1)/√2.
Total variance is λ₁ + λ₂ = 7 + 1 = 8. The first explained variance ratio is λ₁/8 = 7/8 = 0.875 = 87.5%.
examples.answer: The eigenvalues are 7 and 1; the first principal component is along (1, 1)/√2; it explains 87.5% of the total variance.
examples.check:
import math

a = 4.0
b = 3.0
c = 4.0
tr = a + c
det = a * c - b * b
disc = tr * tr - 4.0 * det
l1 = (tr + math.sqrt(disc)) / 2.0
l2 = (tr - math.sqrt(disc)) / 2.0
total = l1 + l2
ratio = l1 / total
print(l1)
print(l2)
print(total)
print(ratio)

traps: PCA uses variance only and ignores class labels. A high-variance direction can be useless for separating classes. Use LDA (Chapter 4.7) when labels exist.
Always mean-centre before PCA. Without centring, the first component may point toward the mean of the data rather than along its spread.
Standardise when features use different units. A feature measured in rupees can dominate a feature measured in metres only because its variance is larger.
The covariance matrix here uses 1/(n−1). Some texts use 1/n; eigenvalues then differ by a constant factor, but the explained variance ratios stay the same.
An eigenvector and its negative are the same direction. Software signs can flip between runs. Do not treat a sign change as a different principal component.

quiz.q: What quantity does the first principal component maximise?
quiz.a: The variance of the projected data. It is the direction with the largest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix.

quiz.q: Why is each feature mean-centred before the covariance matrix is formed?
quiz.a: PCA measures spread around the mean. Without centring, the covariance includes offsets from zero, so a component may point toward the mean rather than along variation.

quiz.q: For C = [[5, 2], [2, 5]], find both eigenvalues and the explained variance ratio of the first component.
quiz.a: Characteristic equation: (5−λ)² − 4 = 0, so λ = 5 ± 2. λ₁ = 7, λ₂ = 3. Ratio = 7/(7+3) = 0.70 = 70%.

quiz.q: Feature x has variance 10⁶ in rupees; feature y has variance 1 in metres. PCA is run without scaling. Predict the first component and explain.
quiz.a: The first component lies almost along x. Its eigenvalue is dominated by the rupee variance, so y contributes little. Standardise if both features should count equally.

quiz.q: X is 100×5 and you keep k = 2 principal components. Give the shapes of V₂ and Z.
quiz.a: V₂ is 5×2. Z = X V₂ is 100×2.

quiz.q: State one difference between PCA and LDA.
quiz.a: PCA is unsupervised and maximises variance. LDA is supervised and maximises between-class separation relative to within-class scatter.

quiz.q: Cumulative explained variance ratios for the first three components are 0.45, 0.60 and 0.90. How many components reach at least 90%?
quiz.a: Three components; the third cumulative ratio is 0.90.

quiz.q: How are eigenvalues of the covariance matrix obtained from the SVD of X?
quiz.a: If X = U S Vᵀ, then the eigenvalues of C are s_i²/(n−1), where s_i is a singular value and n is the number of samples.

beyond: Not for the exam. PCA is the default first step in many data pipelines: image compression, noise removal, and feature extraction before classifiers. In industry, randomized PCA and incremental PCA handle matrices too large for a full eigen-decomposition. Kernel PCA extends the idea to nonlinear structure by applying PCA in a feature space. Search next for singular value decomposition, whitening, kernel PCA and explained variance plots.
